description:
Series 1: Great Crested Flycatcher (Myiarchus crinitus)

16 July 2014: The summer of 2014 was one where the Great Crested Flycatcher (Myiarchus crinitus) made a home during its breeding spring and summer season of the trees in and around Avondale Park and Cooper Creek. All summer long we heard its calls in the treetops, always in the treetops, but the bird itself was a mystery and when you finally found it taking its pic was a whole other question. It took patience and careful watching to figure out what worked best and when to get the images we finally did and once we did we were able to IDentify it. Without question this was the great mystery bird of the summer of 2014 in our own backyard bordering on Avondale Park and Cooper Creek and across the broad expanse of the park itself where its calls were commonplace. Young Great Crested Flycatchers were reared and there were still Great Crested Flycatchers by late August of 2014 in our neighborhood and park. Thus we present two short series of photographs.  The first series is of photographs taken on July 16, 2014, while the second, posted separately immediately following, were taken on August 24, 2014, and these were the result of having attracted the Great Crested Flycatcher with a bit of water and the promise of a cooling bath at the height of the late summer dry season in the North Texas area while watering a part of our backyard. We shared the water with any number of birds late that summer including Great Crested Flycatcher.

Great Crested Flycatcher summers for breeding purposes in the eastern half of the United States including as far west as Texas from its central areas east to the Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana borders and beyond.  In winter Great Crested Flycatcher migrates south through South Texas through Mexico where it both flies through on its way farther south and winters as well in the southeastern states hugging the Gulf of Mexico like Veracruz, Tabasco, Quintana Roo, Chiapas and Yucatán and similarly through wide areas of Central America. Its southernmost range is found in Venezuela and Colombia at the northern end of the South American continent. Because it is a bird that flies from the central and eastern provinces of Canada south through the northern end of South America, Great Crested Flycatcher is an authentic resident of the Western Hemisphere.

Avondale Park and Cooper Creek are administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

Sources:

To see and listen to the calls of the Great Crested Flycatcher click on the following two links borrowed from YouTube:

Great Crested Flycatcher
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EXR5s6HNnrg

And here’s another YouTube video of the Great Crested Flycatcher with different calls: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VOL-DVBkQXc

Finally, see the entry for Great Crested Flycatcher in All About Birds where a good range map and description plus photographs are provided: http://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Great_Crested_Flycatcher/id

No sounds made. Small sized flycatcher that was in tree just above eye level. More of a brownish or olive green, with 2 fairly prominent wing bars evident through bins. Noticed a slightly yellowish wash to the belly as it flew to a 2nd perch, landing facing away. No prominent or perhaps very, very faint eye ring would seem to rule out most other Empids. Initially assumed Acadian as was more expected in location, but the lack of any noticeable eye ring would seem to rule that out as well. Cornell shows an Alder that is very close looking, however didn't notice a strong contrasting white throat (side then back was to me). Nat Geo & Sibley field guides seem to point more to Willow based on the lack of any eye ring and little if any white on throat.

Vireo? Finch? No eye markings, head is plain no eye ring or stripe. Protecting a nest box with 4 newly hatched chicks. Urban environment.

On my daily walk, found a fledgling on the sidewalk. Still too young to fly, the chick needed its nest, but I did not know where it was...until one of the parents flew into a nearby Hackberry tree. During a storm yesterday, one of the tree's rotten branches was at the foot of the trunk. Having picked up the chick and still hearing a chick calling, I turned the broken branch over and discovered the nest and several dead chicks. Securing the other remaining chick from the ground, I obtained help from nearby National Park staff who loaned me a ladder and held the chicks while I returned to my place and picked up tools and wire to make a makeshift nest. I scraped out a cavity, wrapped welded wire around the branch and filled the resultant site with nesting material. The nesting material itself was extremely interesting containing what you see in the photos and bits -both large and small - and pieces of shed snake skin, seen in this observation in the area. 

https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/26140168

This confirms that these birds use shed snake skin in their nests. 

Once I had secured the impromptu nest and replaced the nestlings, we vacated the area then returned a while later to confirm the parents were tending to their offspring. I believe the photos are proof of that supposition.

Ladies and gentlemen: this is where your rare and desirable dragonflies go. To feed another generation of 'fly catchers'.

From the 'about' section on iNaturalist:

"Their breeding habitat is deciduous or mixed forests across eastern North America. They nest in a cavity in a tree. Usually a snake skin is included in the lining of the nest, but sometimes a plastic wrapper is substituted."

I would say many snake skins. The about section also describes the adult birds habitat as in the tops of trees and rarely being seen on the ground. Hunting in the canopy is probably where they find prey.

I would also add, the cavity they use - which I did not see until it hit the ground - was in an old woodpecker cavity. I'm sure they don't make their own.

Location is exactly this tree which is now abandoned, the chicks having fledged. This observation will include photos of parents' vigilance during this stage of the chick's lives. I heard the chick's calls in the bushes around an adjacent house (LBJ National Park), but never observed the babies and did not look too hard as I did not want to draw attention to the chicks and family from tourists nearby. Today I returned and found the parent's guarding the chicks across the street from this location where the riparian vegetation for Town Creek begins. I include a photo of that location as the last one in this series. Bird chicks grow very rapidly, and three days from the time of the nest fall is not unexpected as the baby birds were growing their abdominal feathers complete with yellow breast feathers. The fact that one of the parent birds landed on a branch on the ground near me at Town Creek tells me the chicks had achieved the cover of the creekside habitat. Please enjoy this rescue; it turned out well, imo.

See previous obeservations:

description: Observed by GNA student intern Miranda Davies. The only individual noted. Habitat: Closed-canopy (more or less), secondary hardwood forest with a variety of canopy species. This area was formerly a corn field (until the 1960's). The canopy is composed of a variety of species, with Black Locust (Robinnia pseudoacacia), Box Elder (Acer negundo), and Black Cherry (Prunus serotina) common. Climbers, particularly Oriental Bittersweet (Celastrus orbiculatus) are very common and abundant. The shrub layer is dominated by Autumn Olive (Elaeagnus umbellata), with Multiflora Rose (Rosa multiflora) and Wineberry (Rubus phoenicolasius) very common. The herbaceous layer is dominated by Japanese Stilt Grass (Microstegium vimineum).

description:
With Valeri Ponzo; our second visit to this very cool spot (our first was on 18 May 2012), greatly improving our Columbia County life lists in the process. We parked near the buildings and first walked the entire length of the dike in the middle of the lake. Once we left there (at 1145), we walked Deer Trail then Montgomery Trail to the boardwalk. We then backtracked to Jet. It was surprising what we did NOT see (e.g., Blue-winged Teal, Sandhill Crane, Blue Jay, Tufted Titmouse, Carolina Chickadee, Swamp Sparrow) despite the abundance of suitable habitat. We left at 1216 (after precisely 4 hours!) to go into town for lunch (first stopping but rejecting Subway because the "sandwich artists" were not masked, then going to Hardee's, where the employees were masked).

Not in my field notebook and I don't recall hearing this unseasonal bird, but one "wheep" is clearly audible at the beginning of the recording. I'm guessing that we heard the bird -- or maybe Val heard the bird -- and I got audio of it to document it.
